newsitem.title: UK: Dollar's mettle above 1.50 marks yet to be tested.
newsitem.headline: Dollar's mettle above 1.50 marks yet to be tested.

text.p: The dollar's move above key technical resistance around 1.4965 marks overnight has got many in the market excited about a move into a higher trading range, but the U.S. currency has yet to show it has the conviction. "Now 1.4965 (marks) has broken, it's a question whether the big 1.50 psychological barrier can go as well," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

While it has popped its head above the 1.50 mark parapet trades and analysts are still unsure whether this can hold. In early European business the dollar was trading around 1.4985 after its overnight high of 1.5010, but in later business it had again moved tentatively back above 1.50 marks.

The dollar broke above two-month-old resistance at 1.4965 marks after the European close on Monday, after comments by Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke that there is room for further German repo rate cuts if M3 growth continues to slow. This helped take some of the wind out of the mark's sails and together with a strong performance on Wall Street and in U.S. Treasuries, added up to a rising dollar.

The move higher fills a gap created on July 16 when the dollar dived in reaction to a 161-point fall on Wall Street, the fourth largest one-day loss. The upmove sets up the next target of 1.5030 trendline resistance from a late May peak.

"A monkey with a pencil would have known about this chart point and it certainly wasn't a difficult one to spot," said one trader. "But Europe doesn't seem to want to take it up and this could all quickly run out of steam."
Also the dollar has not gained much ground elsewhere on the foreign exchange so some traders doubt the momentum is there.
There is also the danger that schizophrenic U.S. markets could again change their minds on interest rates and send lofty Wall Street into a spin.
"The big thing about the U.S. market is how swiftly sentiment has shifted," said Chris Tinker, Chief Treasury Economist at Standard Chartered.

Unless Wall Street or Tresuries take off again there seems little on the agenda today to provide the dollar with another major boost. But analysts said that with the market suffering from a severe case of "big figuritis", many will be looking to break back above 1.50 marks and stay there.
"This is all about technicals and not about fundamentals any more," CIBC's Coleman said.

U.S. credit markets have rallied because the Fed is now not expected to tighten as much as had been previously thought. The dollar has rallied because the market thinks the Fed is going to tighten. "Someone is wrong somewhere," Coleman said.
There is no doubt the market desperately wants to see a new trading range, and even though there are some fundamental inconsistencies, a near-term test of the upside is on the cards.

But traders warned there is already a lot of good news for the dollar in the market in terms of official comments and prospects of higher U.S. rates and lower German rates. If it fails to hold 1.50 and above, the market will think again. "The next couple of days is crucial for the dollar," said one trader. "If we can break 1.50 and hold it, we could be into a new trading range of between 1.4950 to around 1.5100-1.5150. Technically, it's crucial be close above 1.4965 marks today."
